blocks.text: Joyfully Seeking the Pure Land, Renouncing the Sahā World

inline.s: (Plain-Language Version)
(For the original text, see
Joyfully Seeking the Pure Land, Renouncing the Sahā World
The sufferings of the Sahā world are too bitter for words; the joys of the Pure Land are too blissful to describe.

Faith, vow, and practice are the three provisions of the Pure Land path. Of these, the vow is to joyfully seek the Pure Land and to renounce the Sahā world. Therefore, while reciting the Buddha's name with diligence, a Pure Land practitioner must also cultivate the practice of joyful seeking and weary renunciation and put it into practice in daily life; this is the concrete expression of faith and vow.

Why should we joyfully seek the Pure Land? Because "the beings in that land have no suffering, but only enjoy every bliss" — and still more, because this is the golden high road that fulfills the bodhi vow to "save all beings and together accomplish the Buddha Way"!
In the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Buddha Sutra, the Buddha says:
Śāriputra, why is that land called Ultimate Bliss? Because the beings in that land have no suffering but only enjoy every bliss, therefore it is called Ultimate Bliss.

As for "all suffering," there are the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, the ten sufferings, and the one hundred and ten sufferings; and there is further the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death (fragmentary birth-and-death and transformative birth-and-death).

The three sufferings are: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the all-pervading suffering of conditioned existence. 1) The suffering of suffering: beings of this world already bear a body subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; when the many afflictions press and scorch them further, suffering is added to suffering — hence "the suffering of suffering." 2) The suffering of change: the suffering felt when a pleasing state that has arisen by chance is lost. 3) The all-pervading suffering of conditioned existence: the suffering of all formations being impermanent, ceaselessly flowing on, never at rest.

The eight sufferings are: 1) the suffering of birth, the pain of coming into the world; 2) the suffering of aging, the pain of years and bodily weakness; 3) the suffering of illness, the pain of sickness; 4) the suffering of death, the pain of the approach of death; 5) the suffering of parting from those we love, the pain of separation from what we cherish; 6) the suffering of meeting those we hate, the pain of being together with enemies; 7) the suffering of not getting what we seek, the pain of desires unfulfilled; 8) the suffering of the blazing five aggregates, in which the illusory body and mind of the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) and all such dharmas give rise to delusion and create karma amid the objects of the six dusts, enduring every torment as though ablaze with fire, unable to cease.

[Five yin] An earlier translation of the five skandhas. Yin means "covering": it can cover over the tathatā and the dharmatā, giving rise to afflictions. [Five skandhas] The skandha of form, the skandha of feeling, the skandha of perception, the skandha of formation, and the skandha of consciousness. Because these five are produced by accumulation, they are called the "five skandhas"; and because they can cover over a person's true nature, causing confusion and inversion and the creation of all kinds of karma, they are also called the "five yin." Of these, the skandha of form refers to matter and is called "form-dharma"; the four skandhas of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called "mind-dharma." These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. The skandha of form is the body, and the other four skandhas (feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) are the mind.
Concerning the ten sufferings and the one hundred and ten sufferings, Master Lianchi says in his Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitābha Sutra:

The ten sufferings: the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Sutra says — 1) the suffering of birth, 2) the suffering of aging, and so on to 10) the suffering of transmigration through birth and death. The one hundred and ten sufferings: the Yogācārabhūmi says — 1) the suffering of undifferentiated transmigration, 2) the suffering of desire, 3) the suffering of delusion, and so on to fifty-five sufferings; then nine kinds of suffering, and within those nine, further opened out in turn into fifty-five, making one hundred and ten in all.

Not one of the sufferings above exists in the Pure Land. As for the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death: one who is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is born by transformation in a lotus, and so has no fragmentary birth-and-death; moreover, one attains the stage of non-retrogression — what need is there to worry about the suffering of transformative birth-and-death? Hence it is said, "there is no suffering."

[Two kinds of birth-and-death] Fragmentary birth-and-death and transformative birth-and-death. [Fragmentary birth-and-death] For beings in the three realms and six paths, because they are impelled by good and evil karma, their life spans all have limits and their bodies all have distinctions; hence their birth and death is called "fragmentary birth-and-death." One who ends fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformative birth-and-death] For the sages of the three vehicles, who have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended fragmentary birth-and-death, in the course of cultivating the path deluded thoughts gradually cease and enlightened realization gradually increases. This shifting of delusion and enlightenment differs with each stage; the passage from one stage into the next is just like a single birth and death, and its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable — hence it is called "transformative birth-and-death." One who ends transformative birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha fruit.
The Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Buddha Sutra
says:
"They enjoy every bliss."
As for "every bliss": the Master of Repentance of Compassionate Cloud, contrasting the sufferings of this land with the joys of that land, lists ten kinds:

1) In this land there is the suffering of not always meeting a Buddha; in that land there is none, but there is the joy of seeing the Buddha as soon as the lotus opens and of always drawing near to him. 2) In this land there is the suffering of not hearing the Dharma; in that land there is none, but there is the joy of water, birds, and trees all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma. 3) There is no suffering of being entangled by evil companions, but there is the joy of all the superior good people gathering in one place. 4) There is no suffering of harassment by hordes of demons, but there is the joy of being protected and remembered by all Buddhas and kept far from demonic affairs. 5) There is no suffering of the unceasing round of rebirth, but there is the joy of cutting across birth-and-death and forever escaping the round of rebirth. 6) There is no suffering of being unable to avoid the three evil paths, but there is the joy of forever leaving the evil paths, whose very names are not heard. 7) There is no suffering of worldly concerns obstructing the path, but there is the joy of enjoying things naturally, with no need to scheme for them. 8) There is no suffering of a short life span, but there is the joy of a life span equal to the Buddha's, without limit. 9) There is no suffering of falling back in practice, but there is the joy of entering the company of the definitely settled and never turning back. 10) There is no suffering of the difficulty of accomplishing the path through dust-kalpas, but there is the joy of completing the practice in one lifetime and accomplishing what is to be done.

[Definitely settled group] One of the three groups. [Three groups] The three groups are three kinds of beings: the definitely settled group, the wrongly settled group, and the unsettled group. The definitely settled group refers to those beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the wrongly settled group refers to those beings who will ultimately not realize enlightenment; the unsettled group refers to those beings between the two, who may or may not realize enlightenment.
[Dust-kalpa] That is,

the three thousand dust-mote kalpas: grind everything in one three-thousand-great-thousand world into ink, and let fall one drop each time you pass through a three-thousand-great-thousand world; when the ink is used up, all the worlds passed through are ground to fine dust, and each mote of dust is counted as one kalpa. This is a simile expressing an extremely long span of time.
The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:

In the Sahā world the conditions and surroundings are turbid and evil; sufferings crowd together and the way is hard to accomplish. In the Pure Land, the land of bliss, all good gathers together and one attains the stage of non-retrogression. Those who invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha are protected and remembered by all Buddhas and are reborn there; those who arouse the bodhi mind are illumined by Amitābha's light and advance. Bodhisattvas and arhats are one's companions; water, birds, and trees all recite the Buddha's name. Wondrous Dharma is always heard at the ear, and greed and anger are suddenly cut off in the mind. Joy is without end; how could the life span have any limit? Once born in that land, one at once attains avaivartika — how unlike the paths of gods and humans, where at every turn so much goes with and against one's wishes. On the road of the provisional vehicles, good roots are rarely complete; the three worthies before the ten grounds have not yet seen the path and already lose their mindfulness. ... From this we know that the followers of the three vehicles pass through asaṃkhyeya kalpas without accomplishing their practice, while through the gate of Buddha-recitation, in the space of a finger-snap, one reaches the stage of non-retrogression. Because those born in the Pure Land are only good and never evil, their stage never recedes and they are certain to become Buddhas. Therefore the Amitābha Sutra says: beings born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avaivartika. Ah! At the outset faith is shallow, and without the power of another it is hard to advance; but our Buddha's vow is deep, and all who have the connection are gathered in. You must believe that learning the way through other gates is like an ant climbing a high mountain, while rebirth in the Pure Land is like a sailboat running with the current. Amitābha Buddha receives and guides one straight to bodhi; the assembled sages lift one up to transcend the three realms. At the highest grade one at once attains the Buddha fruit; even at the lowest birth one still surpasses the heavenly palaces. Believe this universally and do not doubt; cultivate together for non-retrogression.

[Avaivartika] Means "non-retrogression to Buddhahood"; this is an important stage in a Bodhisattva's course of practice. [Provisional vehicles] Provisional-vehicle Bodhisattvas refers to Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka, Shared, and Distinct teachings; because their practice is still shallow, they have not truly reached the rank of a real Bodhisattva. [Three worthies] In the course of Mahāyāna practice, among the fifty-two stages from ordinary being to sage, the Bodhisattvas of the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten dedications have cut off only the delusions of view and thought and still have the delusion of dust-motes and the delusion of ignorance; they have not entered the holy ranks of the ten grounds, and so are called only the "three worthies," or "Bodhisattvas before the grounds."
Master Yinguang taught:
"The sufferings of the Sahā world are beyond words to tell; the joys of the Pure Land are beyond description."

He also drew a sharp contrast between these two worlds and pointed out that one should make a firm and true vow: the vow to leave the sufferings of the Sahā world and the vow to attain the joys of the Pure Land. His teaching runs as follows:

The sufferings of the Sahā world are immeasurable and boundless. In sum, they come down to the eight sufferings: birth, aging, sickness, death, parting from those we love, meeting those we hate, not getting what we seek, and the blazing five aggregates. These eight sufferings belong to everyone, whether one is honored to the highest degree for a time or as lowly as a beggar. The first seven are karmic results incurred in past lives; a little reflection makes them clear, and there is no need to explain them in detail, for to do so would waste far too much ink.

The eighth, "the suffering of the blazing five aggregates," is the present arising of thoughts and stirring of intentions, together with all one's actions and behavior; this is the cause of future suffering. Cause and effect are linked, continuing without break, from kalpa to kalpa, with no escape.

The five yin are form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness. Form is the body that is the karmic retribution incurred; feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness are the illusory, deluded mind that arises on contact with objects. Through this illusory body and mind, one gives rise to delusion and creates karma amid the objects of the six dusts, like a fire blazing up that cannot be stopped — hence "blazing." Further, "yin" is the same as the word meaning "shade": it means covering. These five dharmas cover over the true nature so that it cannot appear. It is like thick clouds hiding the sun: the bright sun's radiance suffers no loss whatever, yet because the thick clouds block it, its light is not received. Just so, ordinary beings who have not cut off delusion and karma are obstructed and covered by these five dharmas (form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness), and the sun of wisdom in the sky of their nature cannot appear. This eighth suffering is the root of all sufferings.

One who cultivates the path and has deep power of meditative concentration has utterly no attachment amid the objects of the six dusts and gives rise to neither hatred nor love. From there, applying effort and advancing, one realizes the unborn, and then delusion and karma are utterly exhausted and the root of birth-and-death is cut off. Yet this work is far from easy; in the Dharma-ending age, those who attain it are truly rare. Therefore one must single-mindedly cultivate the Pure Land karma, seek rebirth in Ultimate Bliss, and relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, be reborn in the West.

Once reborn there, one is born by transformation in a lotus and has no suffering of birth. One has the pure appearance of a youthful man, a life span equal to empty space, and a body free of disaster, change, aging, sickness, and death — their very names are not heard, let alone their reality. One follows the holy assembly and personally attends upon Amitābha; water, birds, and trees all proclaim the sound of Dharma, and each realizes according to his own faculties, attaining realization through hearing. Even those dear to one are utterly unobtainable — how much less could there be enemies? Garments appear as soon as they are thought of, food appears as soon as it is thought of; towers, pavilions, halls, and dwellings are all made of the seven treasures, wrought without human labor, produced by transformation alone. Thus the seven sufferings of the Sahā world are turned into seven joys.

As for the body, one has great supernormal powers and great majestic strength: without leaving one's place, in a single thought one can perform the Buddha's work throughout the Buddha worlds of the ten directions, seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below. As for the mind, one has great wisdom and great eloquence: within one dharma one knows completely the true nature of all dharmas, and expounds the Dharma according to capacities without error. Though one speaks in the language of worldly truth, it accords with the wondrous principle of true reality. One has no suffering of the blazing five aggregates, but enjoys the bliss of the stillness and extinction of body and mind. Hence the sutra says, "There is no suffering, but only the enjoyment of every bliss; therefore it is called Ultimate Bliss."

Knowing now that the Sahā world is suffering and the Pure Land is bliss, one should make a firm and true vow: the vow to leave the sufferings of the Sahā world and the vow to attain the joys of the Pure Land. The urgency of that vow should be like that of one who has fallen into a latrine pit and longs desperately to get out, or of a prisoner in jail who yearns for home.
(Master Yinguang's Record of Excellent Sayings)

blocks.text: When Illness Presses, the Resolve Grows Keener

inline.s: In the Qing dynasty, Master Daoche was a native of Qiantang in Zhejiang. After leaving home, visiting teachers and seeking out friends, and awakening to the mind and seeing the nature, he devoted himself to the Pure Land practice. He lived at Wenshu Hermitage in Hangzhou and set a fixed period
(a prearranged limit)

for a closed retreat. In the retreat room there was nothing superfluous, only a small table and a bed. He had been in retreat only a few days when he fell ill, and the illness grew steadily worse. He spurred himself on, saying: "I entered this retreat to recite the Buddha's name precisely in order to end birth-and-death. How could I break off the retreat to seek medical treatment just because of illness?" So he held the Buddha's name with ever greater earnestness. Before long golden light filled the room, Amitābha Buddha rubbed the crown of his head, and his illness was cured at once.

Thus he attained the Buddha-recitation samādhi, and in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down he had no other thought at all. Three years passed in this way, and on the fifteenth day of the third lunar month he came out of retreat and ascended the seat to expound the Dharma. When he had finished, he told the assembly: "After the fifteenth of the seventh month I shall pass away; you may come to see me off." When the fifteenth of the seventh month came, it was the very day of the Ullambana festival, and the people had gathered together. Someone brought up what he had said earlier about passing away after the fifteenth of the seventh month, and Master Daoche said: "That is so; wait a little while." The next day he handed over the abbotship, prepared a vegetarian feast, and took leave of the assembly. Then he entered his coffin and sat in silence until his breath ceased. After a while he revived and said: "Parting from you all for so long, how could I leave without a word? The sufferings of the Sahā world are too bitter for words; the joys of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are beyond telling. Hold my words firmly in mind: recite Amitābha Buddha's name with single-minded devotion, and before long we shall meet again. If you let slip this great opportunity to be reborn in Ultimate Bliss in this life, you will wander for long kalpas in the round of rebirth. How painful, how painful!" With these words he passed away, at the age of forty-eight.
(Records of Pure Land Sages and Worthies)

[Ullambana festival] "Yulan" is translated into Chinese as "releasing the upside-down." After death, people who fall into the three evil paths suffer extremely, as though hung upside down. "Pen" means a vessel for holding food. "Yulan pen" means: filling vessels with all kinds of precious and delicious foods to offer to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, and relying on the inconceivable power of the field of merit of the Three Jewels to rescue the departed from the suffering of being hung upside down. The "Ullambana festival" is the Dharma assembly held each year on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, at which extensive offerings are prepared and presented to the Three Jewels in order to rescue the departed from the suffering of being hung upside down.
Master Yinguang taught:

When one who recites the Buddha's name falls ill, one should single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name and wait for death. If one's allotted life span is not yet exhausted, one will quickly recover, for reciting the Buddha's name with the whole body and mind let go is the best way to dissolve karma, and when karma is dissolved the illness is cured. If one does not let go but seeks only to be cured, and then fails to recover, one will certainly not be reborn in the Pure Land, because one has no wish for rebirth there. If one does not understand even these principles, how can one rely on the Buddha's compassionate power? As for your mother's illness, you must urge her to let go and seek rebirth. If her allotted span is not yet exhausted, seeking rebirth will instead bring a swift cure, because with a mind of utmost sincerity she will receive the Buddha's compassionate blessing.
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Letter in Reply to Brothers Zhou Mengyou)
Master Shandao taught:

All people who at the end of life seek rebirth in the Pure Land must not fear death. Constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering, entangled in all kinds of impure and evil karma; if one can cast off this defiled body and be born beyond into the Pure Land, enjoying immeasurable bliss and freed from the round of birth and death, that is a matter for rejoicing. It is like taking off ragged clothes and putting on precious and splendid ones. Simply let go of body and mind and do not cling. Whenever illness comes, contemplate impermanence and single-mindedly wait for death.
(Master Shandao's Text on Right Mindfulness at the End of Life for Rebirth in the Pure Land)

[Impermanence] All dharmas in the world arise and cease, shift and flow, never abiding for a single moment; this is called impermanence. Impermanence is the mark of this Sahā world. For living things, plants and animals (humans among them), there is birth, aging, sickness, and death; for inanimate things — minerals, implements, and even mountains, rivers, and the great earth — there is formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness. To know impermanence thoroughly is to understand that whatever is born must cease, whatever gathers must scatter, whatever rises must fall; all things pass, and in the blink of an eye all is empty. Ending birth-and-death is the foremost matter, and one will no longer give rise to craving for pleasing things and situations nor to anger at vexing things and situations — for craving and anger are the root of the round of birth and death. At the same time, to know impermanence thoroughly is to spur oneself at every moment: life is short, the land is fragile; one must seize the time to practice, for when a single breath does not return, one belongs to the next life.
Whatever passes before the eye is reckoned fair or foul; yet in the end not one of them matters at all.

Among the three provisions of the Pure Land path — faith, vow, and practice — the vow is to renounce the Sahā world and joyfully seek the Pure Land. Therefore a reciter of the Buddha's name must not only joyfully seek the Pure Land but also renounce the Sahā world; this is of the greatest importance. Master Xingce, the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, taught:

You must possess a true vow and give rise to the mind of joyful seeking and weary renunciation: regard the three realms as a prison, regard home and family as shackles and manacles, regard sights and sounds as poisonous wine, regard fame and profit as halters and chains, regard the successes and failures of several decades as last night's dream, regard this life as a lodging from which one will soon depart — and with one mind recite the Buddha's name alone, vowing to be born together in the Pure Land.

One who would make his recitation of the Buddha's name not a vain exercise must diligently spur on body and mind, treasuring every inch of time — for life hangs on a single breath, how can it last long? Like a prisoner led to the marketplace, step by step drawing near to death. One must simply press on earnestly
(ceaseless in diligence)
day and night, toiling
kū kū
, unwearied in labor)
through summer and winter, with a single great name, never pausing day or night. In this way one is certain to be born in the Pure Land. Take care not to begin with zeal and end in slackness.
(From Master Xingce's Essential Admonitions)
Old Master Guangqin said:

"If affection and attachment are not cut off, then though you recite the Buddha's name with your lips, every thought still falls back into the Sahā world. If you are earnest and utterly sincere and let go of the ten thousand conditions, then in a single thought you can reach the West. But if the ten thousand conditions tug at you and you cannot let them go, then for a hundred years or ten thousand years you will remain within the three realms."
Then how, amid the tugging of the ten thousand conditions, can one truly renounce the Sahā world? The relevant teachings of the patriarchs are transcribed below.

blocks.text: 1. The Root and Stock of Birth and Death

inline.s: Master Hanshan's Dream Wanderings
"Essential Advice on Buddha-Recitation," teaches:

The Dharma gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is originally for the great matter of ending birth-and-death. Hence it is said: recite the Buddha's name and end birth-and-death. People today arouse the mind and, because they wish to end birth-and-death, are willing to recite the Buddha's name; but they only say, "reciting the Buddha's name can end birth-and-death." If they do not know the root of birth-and-death, where after all are they directing their recitation? If the mind that recites the Buddha's name cannot cut off the root of birth-and-death, how can birth-and-death be ended?
[Root and stock] The root and main stem of a plant; a metaphor for the fundamental basis of a thing.

What is the root of birth-and-death? The ancients said: "If karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if love were not cut off, one would not be born in the Pure Land." From this we know that the root of love is the very root of birth-and-death. For all beings suffer the misery of birth-and-death through the fault of craving and desire. Tracing this root of love, we find it is not something that began in this life, nor in one, two, three, or four lives, but from beginningless time, ever since birth-and-death first was, life after life, casting off the body
(dying)
and receiving a body
(being conceived)

, it is craving and desire that have made one wander on, down to this very day. Looking back, was there ever a single thought that briefly left this root of love? Thus the seeds of this root of love have been accumulated and deepened over countless kalpas, and therefore birth-and-death is without end.
[Love] Means craving, clinging, and defilement.
The Compendium of the Great Vehicle Doctrine says: "Craving and defilement are called love." The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Love is the root of the round of rebirth."
[Root of love] Love produces karmic fruit; hence it is called the root of love.
To chant the Buddha's name is no hard thing; the hard thing is a mind that is one. A mind that is one is no hard thing; the hard thing is to cut the root of love, and have it done.

People today have only just aroused the mind to recite the Buddha's name; they merely look into empty space and seek rebirth in the West, and they do not even know that love is the root of birth-and-death — how could they have cut it off for even a single thought? Since they do not know what the root of birth-and-death is, then while they recite the Buddha's name on the one hand, the root of birth-and-death
(love)

on the other is left free to grow. Reciting the Buddha's name in this way has nothing to do with ending birth-and-death. By such a method, however much you recite, when you come to the end of your life you will only see the root of birth-and-death
(love)
appear before you; only then will you know that your recitation of the Buddha's name has no power at all, and you will complain that recitation is not efficacious — but repentance will come too late.

Therefore I earnestly urge those who recite the Buddha's name today to first understand that love is the root of birth-and-death. In reciting the Buddha's name now, every thought must cut off this root of love. Take the case of one who recites at home: in daily life his eyes see children, grandchildren, family ties, and property, and there is not one thing that is not loved; then there is not one affair, not one thought, that is not the business of birth-and-death — it is as though his whole body were in a pit of fire. Yet he does not know that while he recites the Buddha's name, the root of love in his mind has not been let go for a single thought. He only says, while reciting, that his recitation lacks earnestness, not knowing the reason: love is the master, and recitation is the surface. Reciting in this way, the Buddha's name goes on being recited and love goes on growing. Moreover, when the affection for one's children appears, turn the light around and look: can this single recitation of the Buddha's name really stand against this love? Can it really cut this love off? If it cannot cut this love off, how after all will birth-and-death be ended? For the conditions of love have been thoroughly familiar through many lives, while recitation of the Buddha's name is newly begun and utterly unfamiliar, and it is neither earnest nor substantial; hence it has no power.
[Conditions of love] Love
as a condition. The Ratnakūṭa Sutra says: "Among all afflictions, those joined by the conditions of love are the heaviest."

If you cannot take charge even of the objects of love before you now, then at the end of your life you will certainly not be able to take charge. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name: above all, know that the mind to end birth-and-death must be urgent. Knowing that the mind to end birth-and-death must be urgent, you must, upon the root of birth-and-death
(the root of love)
cut it off with every thought; then every thought is the time for ending birth-and-death. Why wait until the thirtieth of the twelfth month
(the end of life)

before ending birth-and-death? If you think of ending birth-and-death only then, it is far, far too late. As it is said: "Before your eyes all is the matter of birth-and-death; end the birth-and-death before your eyes, and birth-and-death is empty." With every thought so earnest, every stroke drawing blood, if one applies the mind in this way and still does not escape birth-and-death, then all the Buddhas would have uttered false speech. Therefore, whether householder or monk, so long as one truly has the mind to end birth-and-death, that is the season for escaping birth-and-death — what other wondrous method could there be?

[Before your eyes all is the matter of birth-and-death; end the birth-and-death before your eyes, and birth-and-death is empty] Before your eyes is all the business of birth-and-death; when you have finished with this business of birth-and-death before your eyes, you have ended birth-and-death (birth-and-death is empty).

blocks.text: 2. Cutting Off Love and Unifying the Thought

inline.s: [Cutting off love and unifying the thought] To cut off love and make the thought one. [To cut off love and make the thought one] To cut off the root of love and make the thought of reciting the Buddha's name single and undivided.
Master Youxi, in his Pure Land Dharma Words, teaches:

Yet as for seeking rebirth in the Pure Land: to speak of it is not difficult, but to practice it in earnest is difficult. To practice it in earnest is not difficult, but to awaken to the essential heart of the practice is difficult. This is what the ancients warned of, and we should respectfully follow it. If you would obtain the most earnest instruction for your own practice
(the essential heart)
, nothing surpasses Yang Cigong's two phrases: "If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā world; if the thought is not one, one is not born in Ultimate Bliss."

[Yang Cigong] Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, style name Wuweizi. A man of the Song dynasty. He was at first fond of Chan and greatly awakened while studying under Chan Master Tianyi Huai. At the end of the Xining era he returned home to observe mourning for his mother (his mother's death). Living in leisure, he read the Buddhist canon and thereupon turned his heart to the Pure Land, vigorously promoting it, and painted a sixteen-foot image of Amitābha Buddha to contemplate wherever he went. At the end of his life he saw a golden platform descend from the sky, spoke a verse, and passed away. [If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā world] To end birth-and-death and escape the round of rebirth, one must cut off love. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All beings, from beginningless time, because of various kinds of love, affection, and craving, have the round of rebirth." [If the thought is not one, one is not born in Ultimate Bliss] To be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must make the thought of reciting the Buddha's name single and undivided. The single, undivided thought of reciting the Buddha's name is what the Chapter on Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva calls "pure thoughts succeeding one another," and what Master Shandao calls "thought after thought continuing without interruption."

Reciting the Buddha's name is for the sake of making the mind single. Therefore to hold the name earnestly and concentrate the mind without distraction is what one should strive at with all one's heart. Yet sometimes one forgets and does not recite, and sometimes one recites but cannot make it one; there is no other reason — it is affection and love that have dragged the mind of recitation away
(giving rise to wandering thoughts)

. To lighten love so as to cut off wandering thoughts, to sever the root of affection, and to escape the net of love — this is what one should strive at with all one's heart. Yet sometimes one recites but cannot forget love, and sometimes one wishes to forget love but cannot forget it entirely; there is no other reason — it is because the mind of recitation cannot be single. Therefore, for one who recites the Buddha's name and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land: if in daily life there is a single love of the Sahā world that is not let go, then at the end of life one will be dragged by that love and will not be reborn — how much more so if there are many loves? If in seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is a single thought that is not single-minded, then at the end of life one will be turned about by that distracted thought and will not be reborn — how much more so if there are many distracted thoughts?

As for what love is: it may be light or heavy, thick or thin; it may concern the direct retribution or the circumstantial retribution. To list its kinds: there are parents, wife and children; brothers and friends; rank and wealth; essays and poems; arts and skills; clothing and food; houses and fields; woods, springs, and flowers; precious jewels and playthings — all manner of excellent and lovely things, too many to enumerate one by one. Among them, some are great and heavy as Mount Tai, some small and light as a goose feather. To be unable to forget a single thing is love; to be unable to let go a single thought is love. If a single love dwells in the breast, the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is not one; if a single thought is not gathered into one, one will not be reborn in Ultimate Bliss.

Alas! These two phrases — "If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā world; if the thought is not one, one is not born in Ultimate Bliss" — may be called a golden scalpel to scrape away the film from the eye, a sovereign remedy for a disease past cure. All who aspire to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should write these two phrases on their walls and engrave them on their flesh, reciting them solemnly at every moment and keeping them before the mind in every thought. As for the loves of the Sahā world, seek daily to lighten them; as for the thought of Ultimate Bliss, seek daily to make it one. Lighten love again and again until it is gone; unify the thought again and again until it reaches the ultimate. If one can truly do so, then though such a person has not yet left the Sahā world, he is no longer a long-staying guest of the Sahā world; and though he has not yet been born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, he is already an honored guest of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. With right mindfulness present at the end of life, rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is certain.

[The golden scalpel that scrapes the film from the eye] The golden scalpel (jīn pī), also written jīn bī, was an instrument used in ancient times to treat eye disease; with it one scraped away the film on the surface of the eyeball and restored sight. [Past cure] Refers to an incurable disease.

Someone asked: Is there a method for lightening love? The answer: The key to lightening love is to make the thought one. He asked again: Is there a method for making the thought one? The answer: The key to making the thought one is to lighten love. The man laughed and said: Master, your words waver and have no firm ground, leaving the student at a loss. The answer: It is not that they waver; this is to make clear the reason why the thought is made one. For the thought
(the thought of reciting the Buddha's name)

cannot be single because the mind scatters and strays after other things. That the mind scatters and strays after other things is because it chases after objects in confusion. Therefore, for every object in the Sahā world there is a mind in beings; for every mind in beings there is an object in the Sahā world. Hence it is said: "When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when dharmas arise, all minds arise." Conditions gather and the mind arises; it races after objects, the mind clinging to objects and objects pulling the mind, mind and objects chasing each other, and even dust-mote kalpas cannot exhaust it. If love is not cut off, can the thought be single?
Therefore, one who would make the thought one had best lighten love; one who would lighten love had best make the mind one. One who would make the mind one had best shut off its objects
(so that the mind does not cling to objects)
; when all objects are empty, the ten thousand conditions are all still; when the ten thousand conditions are all still, the single thought accomplishes itself
(then the pure, single thought of the Buddha naturally comes to accomplishment)

. If the single thought is accomplished, the conditions of love are all exhausted. Hence it is said: "Would you make the thought one? Best lighten love. Would you lighten love? Best make the thought one." For the conditions of love and the singleness of thought cannot both stand, like night and day succeeding each other, or like darkness and light utterly opposed.
(Thus, cutting off love and making the thought one support and complete each other.)
Question: In letting go of the ten thousand conditions and single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, is one concerned only with one's own benefit?
Answer: Master Yinguang says:

"Before one can save oneself, to wish to save others — how is that different from ferrying people while drowning in the sea? I earnestly urge all worthy ones not to let arrogance grow tall, but rather to have true faith and urgent vows, and relying on compassionate power, recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West."
(Buddha-Recitation Instruction at Fazang Temple, Shanghai)
[Self-admonition] Warning oneself. In these seven articles of self-admonition, Master Lianchi clearly sets out the things that must not be done, in order to keep the single mind of right mindfulness.
Master Lianchi's Posthumous Manuscripts of Master Yunqi
"Self-Admonition," says:

The ancients said: "Even Great Yu, a sage, treasured every inch of time; we should treasure every fraction of an inch." Now that I am old and my body weak, must I treasure merely each fraction of an inch? Not even for the space of a finger-snap may I let the mind be distracted!

"Not to let the mind be distracted" means that apart from one's fundamental contemplation and right mindfulness, as soon as a single distracting thought arises it must at once be swept away and gathered back into right mindfulness, without a moment's delay. Here I briefly list seven matters; those who have truly left home for the sake of birth-and-death and wish to settle the great matter in this one life must do their utmost to observe them and admonish themselves at all times.

[Fundamental contemplation and right mindfulness] Master Lianchi cultivated Buddha-recitation samādhi through inquiry, so his fundamental contemplation and right mindfulness is "Amitābha Buddha." Master Lianchi says: "Raising a huatou is the most urgent work for awakening in the Chan school. One who cultivates the Pure Land should simply take a single recitation of the Buddha's name as a huatou — this is the wondrous method." He also says: "When wandering thoughts fly in confusion, simply raise the Buddha's name lightly once and then stop, and look: who is it that recites the Buddha's name? After a long while, when a thought arises (when a deluded thought arises), raise it and look in the same way; if no thought arises, simply watch."
(Collected Pure Land Sayings of Yunqi) On the inquiry into Buddha-recitation and Buddha-recitation samādhi, see in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Record of Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation Samādhi

One. Do not hoard wealth, build houses, buy fields, or procure all manner of fine objects. Even scriptures and images handed down from the most ancient times—though they come from celebrated hands—must not be cherished; keep your single thought of Right Mindfulness.

[Single-minded Right Mindfulness] Master Lianchi says: “One who is determined to learn has but a single right thought ever present in his breast. In quiet moments it is so; in noisy moments it is so too. Let stillness and clamor shift as they may, that thought of mine is by no means moved; only then is there no interruption, and this is called doing the work well. Have you not seen the ancients say: The wise person removes the mind; the foolish person removes the environment. If one must shun noise and seek stillness, then I fear there is never a time of stillness in the world, nor any place of stillness. One who seeks stillness would do best to go deep among the mountains. Yet the mountains are still, and the woodcutter’s axe is heard across the cloud, the herdsman’s flute sounds in the slanting sun—how then can the ear be still? The woodcutter’s axe and the herdsman’s flute might perhaps be shut out so that they do not reach my ear; but on clear nights the apes cry and the tigers roar, and by day the magpies chatter and the crows caw—how can it then be still? The apes’ cries and the tigers’ roars, the magpies’ chatter and the crows’ caws might perhaps be driven away so that they do not reach my ear; but when a wild wind rises and the ten thousand hollows roar together, and a sudden thunderclap shakes a thousand mountains, then will one who shuns noise and seeks quiet shut them out? Will he drive them away? By this reasoning, the world surely has no time of stillness, and surely no place of stillness. The student needs only to fear that his resolve is not fierce enough! If he holds a fierce resolve, where can he go that is impossible?” (Collected Teachings of Yunqi)

Two. Do not undertake all manner of unimportant meritorious works; wait until the great matter is clear, and then it will not be too late to do them. For now, lay aside the gate of the myriad practices and keep your single thought of Right Mindfulness.

[The great matter] Here it means seeing one’s nature and awakening to the mind. For a reciter of the Buddha’s name who has not yet reached single-mindedness without scattering, attaining that single-mindedness is the foremost great matter of putting an end to birth and death. [The gate of the myriad practices] “Myriad practices” refers to all methods of practice; “gate” carries the meaning of entering and going forth. Chan Master Guishan Lingyou says: “In the ground of ultimate principle not a single mote of dust is received; within the gate of the myriad practices not a single dharma is forsaken.” (Record of Chan Master Guishan Lingyou of Tanzhou)

Three. Do not let greed and attachment arise toward pleasing sights and fine flavors, nor toward those who speak well of me and praise me. Do not let anger and vexation arise toward ugly sights and spoiled flavors, nor toward those who speak ill of me, slander me, revile and insult me, or in all manner of ways cross me. Even the affairs of the past and the future, whether favorable or adverse, must all be cast off and cut off utterly, giving rise to no thoughts of love or hate, of grasping or rejecting. Hold fast like a walled fortress, and keep your single thought of Right Mindfulness.
[Fortified wall] A firm and unshakeable rampart.
Four. Do not compose poetry or write essays, or pen in regular script
(the true script)

or in cursive script inscriptions, couplets, and scrolls, nor embellish your letters and leaf through outside books. Do not discuss others’ gains and losses, strengths and weaknesses, nor, trusting solely to your own private view, with self-righteousness
(lofty conceit)

compose works. While your Chan is not yet thoroughly awakened, you must not recklessly take up ancient cases to comment on and extol; you should seal your lips and hold your tongue, and abide in single-minded Right Mindfulness.

[Outside books] The Buddha’s canonical teachings are the inner canon; all books beyond these are called outside books. [Taking up and commenting] This refers to “taking up the ancient” and “commenting and extolling.” “Taking up the ancient” means bringing out an ancient case or kōan to awaken a student of Chan; “commenting and extolling” means appraising and putting forth the sayings of the ancients.

Five. Do not befriend relatives and close friends, attend invitations and other social engagements, wander the mountains and admire the scenery, or engage in idle talk of every kind. As for the various worldly affairs, apart from what is right and proper to do and absolutely cannot be declined, set all the rest aside, and keep your single thought of Right Mindfulness.

Six. Do not crave and cling, or let body and mind run loose and give way to sleep. So long as the great matter is not clear, you must labor diligently and endure hardship, keeping your single thought of Right Mindfulness.

Seven. Do not contend with the world over talents, or strive for fame and power, or, not having attained, claim attainment, and not having realized, claim realization, falsely calling yourself a good teacher and thinking yourself superior. You should only hold to humility and guard your foolishness, remain a student all your life, and train yourself, advancing with diligence without ceasing, keeping your single thought of Right Mindfulness.

[Not having attained, claiming attainment; not having realized, claiming realization] Not having attained the noble Dharma, one yet claims to have attained it; not having realized the fruit of the Way, one yet claims to have realized it.

In the Qing dynasty there was an old lady known as “Caring for Nothing.” Her name is unknown; all one knows is that she was a native of Hangzhou. She once asked Master Daoyuan of the Temple of Compassion and Kindness: “What method of practice can, in a single lifetime, surely free one from the sea of suffering?” Master Daoyuan replied: “There is nothing better than reciting the Buddha’s name! Yet reciting is not difficult; what is difficult is
lasting persistence
; and persistence is not difficult; what is difficult is
single-mindedness

. If you can set aside all worldly affairs, single-mindedly invoke the Buddha’s name, and with a sincere heart vow to be reborn there, then when death comes the Buddha will appear to guide you, and you will escape the sea of suffering!” The old lady joyfully bowed in thanks. Upon returning home she entrusted the household affairs to her daughters-in-law, prepared a pure chamber, enshrined a Buddha image within it, and cultivated there.

After more than a year, she came again to ask Master Daoyuan: “Since I received your instruction, your disciple has given up household duties and applied himself single-mindedly to reciting the Buddha’s name. I consider myself able now to recite persistently without slackening, yet I am tormented that single-mindedness is too hard and that I cannot reach it. Please teach me again what I should do.” Master Daoyuan said: “Although you have cast off household affairs, you still harbor concern for your children, grandchildren, and relatives. If this root of love is not pulled up, how can single-mindedness be achieved? Now, to carry your practice a step further, you must first pull out the root of love, let go of everything, and only then can you attain single-mindedness!” The old lady sighed and said: “The master speaks entirely rightly! Although my body no longer manages things, within my heart I have still not let go. From now on, I will truly be a person who cares for nothing!” Thereupon she became even more diligent. Whenever a stirring of affection arose, she would at once silently recite the words “Caring for Nothing” and drive it away. When anyone asked her about household affairs, she likewise refused them with those words, “Caring for Nothing.” Thus her great reputation “Caring for Nothing” spread among relatives, friends, and the villagers. More than a year passed in this way, until one day she came to the Temple of Compassion and Kindness, bowed in thanks to Master Daoyuan, and said: “The master did not deceive me; in a few days your disciple must depart for the West!” A few days later she passed away without illness. (The original text is found in The Essentials of Reciting the Buddha’s Name.)

On New Year’s Eve of the year yǐchǒu of the Jiājìng reign (1565), Master Lianchi bade his wife Lady Tang to brew tea. As Lady Tang carried the tea to the table, she let it slip and it fell to the ground. Seeing his beloved heirloom jade cup shatter, the master laughed and said:
“There is no principle whereby causes and conditions do not dissolve.”

The following year he bid Lady Tang farewell, saying: “Loving affection cannot last forever; in birth and death none can take another’s place. I am going to leave the home life; arrange your own affairs well.” Lady Tang likewise replied with ease: “Go on ahead, sir. Once I have settled matters at home, I too will leave the home life.” The master then composed the lyric “Erased in One Stroke” and left the home life.

[Erased in a single stroke] This is an expression the ancients used for settling accounts, meaning to wipe away a debt that has been paid off with one stroke; later it was extended to mean canceling everything entirely. For example, the late Tang Daoist Lü Dongbin, in his poem of awakening “Qinyuanchun,” says: “Cease, cease; turn back early, and erase with one stroke the gallantry of former days.”

The grace of parents is weighty as the hills; / Five tripods and the threefold beasts cannot repay. / Both parents must be saved from birth and death, / And then a child’s filial way is fulfilled. / Chā! This great cause of leaving the home life— / How can the worldly knowledge of ordinary beings fathom it through? / A true filial son and worthy descendant should inquire into the reality of all dharmas (for one must attain the Way oneself to free one’s parents from the sea of birth and death); / Therefore the five-colored golden insignia that brings honor to parents and luster to ancestors is erased in one stroke.

[Five tripods and the threefold beasts] A description of sacrificial offerings of the utmost abundance. [Five tripods] In ancient times, when a sacrifice was offered, a great officer used five tripods. [Threefold beasts] The ox, the sheep, and the pig. [When one’s parents are freed from the dust, then a child’s way is fulfilled] This means: only when one’s parents have escaped birth and death (departed from the dust of defilement) is a child truly fulfilling filial piety. [Chā] An exclamation; here it is a shout to jolt one awake. [True emptiness] The reality of all dharmas. [The reality of all dharmas] The actual condition of all dharmas. The Buddha Treasury Sutra says: “What is called the reality of all dharmas? Namely, all dharmas are ultimately empty, having no existence.” (See in detail
“The Reality of All Dharmas”
.) [Five-colored golden insignia] The court robes of high officials in ancient times; here it refers to achieving fame and success, bringing honor to one’s parents, and glorifying one’s ancestors.

Master Hanshan says: “Throughout the world, what parents hope of their children is that they will win renown to honor them, and so they take the support of the three beasts and five tripods to be the fullness of filial piety. Little do they know that the more lavish the support, the deeper the suffering—that is to burden one’s parents, not to be truly filial. Therefore our Buddha, the World-Honored One, thought lightly of the golden wheel (disdaining the throne of the Golden-Wheel king) and did not take it. He abandoned his parents, forsook the palace, and practiced austerities in the snow mountains, attaining the Way in six years and becoming the honored one of the three worlds, looked up to by gods and humans. If he had not given up the supremely noble and severed the great love, how could he have won the deathless career that lasts through long kalpas? Hence it is said: “Greatly filial is the Buddha of the Śākya clan, repaying his parents’ kindness through countless kalpas.” Is this not taking the realization of the unborn and the universal salvation of beings as the ground of repayment? In the Buddha’s great precepts the first is: filial piety is called the precept—meaning to be filial to one’s parents, filial to the teachers, elders, and the Three Jewels, filial to the ultimate Way, and filial to all living beings. Therefore, one who truly studies and practices the Buddha’s Dharma regards all sentient beings as his parents from many lives—how could he fail to repay the grace of the parents of this single life (how could he fail to repay the kindness of his parents in this present life)?” (Dream Wandering Collection · An Address to the Layman Wang Ziyi on Renouncing the Home Life)

Phoenix mates and lovebirds, / When will this tangled love and longing end? / Are they not but living ghosts, all dressed and painted, clinging to each other, / And when the karma is spent, they part. / Chā! For your sake—this passionate tenderness— / One wears the cangue and the locks, wandering the rivers and lakes. / See through it: you are a creditor come to exact a debt; / Each should seek the gate of liberation and go. / Therefore the husband and wife as close as fish to water are erased in one stroke.

[Phoenix mates and lovebirds] A reference to the fondness between a man and a woman, in harmony as a phoenix and a luan bird paired together. [Niŭ] An ancient instrument of restraint resembling handcuffs. [Chóu móu] Deep affection and lingering tenderness: the passion between two lovers. [Creditor] A foe who comes to exact vengeance. “A husband and wife are creditors” means that each holds the other fast, endlessly suffering in the round of birth and death. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “You love my mind, I pity your form; because of this cause and condition we pass through a hundred thousand kalpas, ever bound together.” The remedy is to enter the gate of liberation, and from being lovers to become fellow practitioners on the Way. [Each seeking the gate to go] Each seeks for himself the gate (the Buddhist gate) by which to escape birth and death.

The body is filthy and bitter as a festering sore; / Do not make far-reaching worries for children and grandchildren. / Remember of old how Yanshan taught his five sons, / Whose fame spread through the world—but are they here today? / Chā! In the end there is a time to stop; / In the end it comes to having no descendants at all; / Alone one walks the road of the Yellow Springs. / Who recognizes this very person
(one’s own nature)
, / Unchanging through the ages as of old
(never old, never dying)
? / Therefore the osmanthus branch and the orchid grandson are erased in one stroke.

[Dou of Yanshan] That is Dou Yujun, a man of the later Jin of the Five Dynasties, whose old home was Yuyang in Jizhou, in the region of Mount Yan. Later generations therefore honored him as Dou Yanshan, following the ancient custom of showing respect by referring to a man by his native place. His family discipline was very strict; he had five sons, all excellent in both learning and conduct, praised in their day as the “Five Dragons of the Dou Clan,” and all passed the imperial examination to become pillars of the state. The Trimetric Classic says: “Dou Yanshan had a righteous way; he taught five sons, and all their names were made known.” [Are they here today?] “Where are the generals and ministers of ancient and modern times? A heap of wilderness graves, swallowed by the grass.” [In the end no descendants] When one breath ceases, one walks the Yellow Springs alone; in the final analysis, who has any children or descendants? [Who recognizes this very person] Who knows that one’s own nature is one’s true self? Sentient beings are deluded and mistakenly take the physical body for the self, not knowing that their own nature is the true self, and so there is birth and death and the round of transmigration. The

Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, from beginnings time onward, are in all manner of inversion, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions (taking east for west, south for north, and so on), who wrongly take the four great elements to be the self and the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects to be the mind. They are like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon…… Because of this there arises the false revolving in birth and death, and this is called ignorance.”

[The four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has the nature of hardness, water of wetness, fire of warmth, and wind of movement. All the material, formed things in the world possess these four natures—hard, wet, warm, moving—and so they are called “great.” The physical body is composed of the four elements; here “the four great elements” refers to the physical body. [The shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-organs touch the six sense-objects; and since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects—the illusory shadows produced by contact with the six sense-objects. [Osmanthus branch and orchid grandson] A complimentary name for a person’s children and grandchildren. When children and grandchildren are at once honorable and flourishing, this is called the orchid and osmanthus in bloom together.

Standing alone on the turtle’s head, / Do not say this is a man’s hour of triumph. / The golden seal hangs large as a bushel; / Power and prestige cannot long endure. / Chā! How many have run to and fro in vain; / Youthful cheeks in a twinkling turn to white hair. / Wake from the dream of yellow millet, / And smile to see—what remains? / Therefore wealth, honors, and fame are erased in one stroke.

[Standing alone on the turtle’s head] The “turtle’s head” is the bas-relief of the giant turtle on the steps before the palace gates. When the list of successful candidates was posted at the imperial examination, the top scholar would stand upon it to receive the announcement. [How many have run to and fro in vain] “Where are the generals and ministers of old? A heap of wilderness graves, swallowed by the grass.” (Scene from The Red Chamber Dream, “The Song of Good and Enough”) [The dream of yellow millet] The allusion comes from the Tang-dynasty Pillow Record: “In the seventh year of the Kaicheng reign there was a man named Lu Ying, styled Zuizhi. At an inn in Handan he met a Daoist, the Old Man Lü. When the young man sighed in self-pity over his poverty and straitened circumstances, the Old Man took a pillow from his bag and gave it to him, saying, ‘If you rest upon this pillow, it will bring you honor and satisfaction.’ At that moment the innkeeper was steaming millet; the young man bowed his head and slept, and in his dream entered the pillow and arrived at his own home. Within a few months he took a daughter of the Cui clan of Qinghe as his wife. The girl was very lovely, and her dowry grew ever richer, and the man rejoiced greatly. Soon after, he passed the imperial examination, rose office by office to be a household attendant, was made a military governor, routed the barbarian raiders in a great victory, and served as prime minister for more than ten years. His five sons all held office, and his ten-odd grandchildren married into the most distinguished families of the age; he lived to be over eighty, and then died. When he awoke, the millet was not yet cooked. Astonished, he said, ‘Could this have been a dream?’ The Old Man smiled and said, ‘The satisfactions of human life are just like this.’ The young man, dazed and at a loss, remained a long while, then bowed his head in reverence and took his leave.” [Yellow millet] Huangliang, the yellow grain of millet. [Bowing the head to the ground] To kneel, fold the hands down to the earth, and bring the head to the ground.

Richer than princes and marquises, / You say I rejoice; I say I grieve. / In the seeking I suffered every bitterness, / And once gained, I dread its overthrow. / Chā! Plain tea and simple rice surpass rare delicacies; / A patched robe and a worn jacket are as brocade. / Between heaven and earth is my home; / Why raise for myself a great mansion? / Therefore house, land, and fields are erased in one stroke.

[You say I rejoice; I say I grieve] You think that, being richer than princes and marquises, I must be full of joy; you do not know the bitterness within: to pursue wealth I suffered every hardship; and once I have, by good fortune, grown rich, I am forever anxious lest the officials, thieves, floods, fire, and a spendthrift son destroy my riches. [Suffering] To endure hardship; toil.

The sea of learning flows on without a pause; / One’s light in the world of letters shoots to the Dipper and the Ox; / Through the hundred arts one roams at will, / A bushel of wine and a thousand poems. / Chā! With brocade filling the breast and the head, / Why need you boast? / Before birth and death, / Not a single thread can save you. / Therefore world-surpassing literature is erased in one stroke.
[The sea of learning] In Yang Xiong of the Han dynasty’s Model Sayings

“On Learning and Conduct”: “A hundred streams study the sea and so reach the sea; hills study the mountain but do not reach the mountain.” This means: a hundred streams flow ceaselessly, and so they reach the sea; hills rest without moving, and so they do not reach the mountain. Therefore in study one should be like a river flowing to the great sea, advancing daily without cease. [The literary field] The world of letters.
[The light of the literary field shoots to the Dipper and the Ox] A description of how great this person’s talent is: in the world of letters the light shines out ten thousand fathoms,
shooting up to the Dipper constellation (the Big Dipper) and the Ox constellation (Altair).

In summer admiring, in spring rambling, / Amid song and dance the pleasures crowd thick; / Mist and rain have veiled the flowers and willows; / Tea, wine, lute, and chess delight kin and friends. / Chā! Now everyone shows off his elegance, / But the bitterness falls on one’s own self after death. / How pitiable to waste the daylight and miss the great matter of birth and death, / With regret and shame unbearable, looking back in vain; / Therefore feelings of love and romance are erased in one stroke.

[Now] Under the eyes; at present; at this very moment. [Elegant] Possessing both achievements and literary grace. [Mǒ luó] A Sanskrit word, rendered into Chinese as “shame” [remorse]. [Looking back in vain] Recalling past events—all empty.

Time passes swiftly, and human life is impermanent. One who studies the Buddha’s way must be vigilant at every moment; never treat the matter lightly, amusing yourself and sporting, casting away time, only to regret without end. The verse of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, “Warning the Assembly,” says: “This day has already passed, and life diminishes with it, like a fish with but little water—what joy is there in this? All of you: be diligent in exertion, as if saving your heads from burning! Only be mindful of impermanence (mindful of the coming of death), and by no means be idle (never give way to ease and pleasure).”
[A fish with little water] A fish in a pool whose water dries up day by day.
[Be diligent in exertion, as if saving your head from burning]
A great fire is blazing on your head and death is fast approaching; in reciting the Buddha’s name you should
be diligent and untiring,
hastening
without a moment’s delay, to extinguish this fire of death, and, before you fall into a coma and die, accomplish the ten successive recitations so that they become a settled habit (see in detail
“The Conditions for Rebirth”

). [Impermanence] Whatever does not abide (all things in the world arise and cease, flowing on, without dwelling even for an instant); it also refers to death and to the spirit that summons the soul. [

By no means be idle] Never indulge in ease and pleasure so as to waste your energy and time. The Buddha said: “Though one labors diligently for a single lifetime, in an instant one will be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with joy beyond measure.” (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)
Thus it is:
In life one exhausts a thousand wiles and myriad schemes; / In death one leaves behind only a pair of empty hands.
Grief and joy, parting and reunion make a din each morning; / Long and short of life, poverty and wealth keep one busy every day.
Cease contending for strength and vying for superiority; / A hundred years is but a stage for plays.
In a moment the gong and drum fall silent; / Who knows where one will make one’s exit?
[In a moment the gong and drum fall silent]
In a flash impermanence arrives, and this play is finished (the gong and drum fall silent).
